Where it began

Marcus Trescothick was born in Keynsham, Somerset, on Christmas Day 1975, and grew up around the town's cricket club. He was handed his first bat before his first birthday, and it seems to have taken. Playing for the Avon under-11 side he made 124 against Devon, then was unbeaten on 183 a couple of weeks later when the coach decided enough was enough and declared.

At 14 he was in the England under-14 side with Andrew Flintoff and Paul Collingwood. He went on to captain England's under-19s and first played for Somerset in 1993.

The player

Duncan Fletcher noticed him in 1999, when he made 167 against Fletcher's Glamorgan side in a low-scoring game where nobody else passed 50. A year later Fletcher was England coach, and Trescothick was in the team. He played 76 Tests between 2000 and 2006, scoring 5,820 runs at 43.76 with 14 hundreds and 29 fifties.

His best was 219 against South Africa at The Oval in 2003. He passed 1,000 Test runs in three calendar years running, from 2003 to 2005, and in the Ashes summer of 2005 he became the quickest man to reach 5,000 Test runs. He led England in two Tests, winning one and losing one.

What made him special

He hit the ball very hard. His feet did not always move far, but his timing and strength carried the ball a long way, and he was at his best against spin, as a fine tour of India in 2001 showed. His opening stands with Andrew Strauss gave England many good starts, including 273 together at Durban.

He was a superb catcher at slip, with 95 Test catches. In 2018 he caught all three victims of a Craig Overton hat-trick against Nottinghamshire, which had happened only twice before in first-class cricket.

A Somerset man

After his England years came a long and happy chapter at Taunton. In 2007 he made a career-best 284 against Northamptonshire. In 2009 he topped the County Championship run list with 1,817, and from 2010 he captained Somerset for six seasons. In 2010 he also hit a fifty from 13 balls, the fastest in English domestic Twenty20 cricket at the time. In 2017 he passed Harold Gimblett for the most first-class hundreds for Somerset.

He retired at the end of 2019, after more than 26 seasons with the county, and left the field at Taunton to a standing ovation and a guard of honour from Essex. He went on to coach England's Test batsmen, and in 2024 had a spell as interim head coach of the white-ball side.

And finally

He was known as Tresco, and also as Banger, after a youthful diet that seldom strayed far from sausages. Keynsham gave him the Freedom of the town in 2005, and he picked up an MBE in 2006 and an OBE in 2024. A keen golfer, he was also made an honorary vice-president of Bristol City.
